newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Russia tempts bond mkt with bright future.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia tempts bond mkt with bright future.

text.p: Russia, predicting a rosy future for its economy, said on Friday it hoped its first visit to the international capital markets since the 1917 revolution would bring it respectability among the world's investors.
The Eurobond issue would allow Russia to tap another source of funds to pay for its budget deficit, currently heavily dependent on International Monetary Fund (IMF) loans.

"The purpose for entering this market is not a short-term goal, it is for the long term," Finance Minister Alexander Livshits told a news conference before meeting London-based investors to drum up support for the bond.
"We want from the outset to look respectable," he said.
Russian officials were upbeat after the first week of a hectic schedule of presentations to investors around the globe.
"The results so far seen quite satisfactory," Livshits said. "The response (from investors) has been warm and they liked what we presented."

He pointed to success so far in turning Russia into a market economy, lowering inflation and interest rates and predicted growth next year would reach one percent after sharp falls since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Russia has already gone some way to rehabiliate its reputation in the international arena with agreements to reschedule most of the old Soviet debt to the West.
But Livshits warned that the process of transition was not getting any easier.

The government is embroiled in tough negotiations with the IMF which has delayed payment of part of a $10 billion loan until Moscow proves it can bring in enough tax revenue to fund government spending.
Moscow has said it hopes the IMF will pay out the money before the end of the year, aware that it will not be able to finance this year's budget deficit without the money.
This month also sees hard bargaining in the Russian parliament to agree the 1997 budget before the end of the year.
"There is still a possibility that the budget for 1997 will be approved this year," Livshits said, though deputies in Moscow have been less optimistic.
The Eurobond will pave the way for Russian borrowers, such as the cities of Moscow and St Petersburg, and companies like Gazprom and LUKoil to go to the markets for funds next year.
Terms of the deal, expected to be for up to $500 million for between three and five years, would not be determined until presentations to investors end in New York on November 20, Livshits said.
Though international borrowing was expected to continue next year, the domestic market would remain its main source of funds.
"In 1997 the government would like to borrow on the international market as a reliable and sustainable source of borrowing," Livshits said.

Russia's new bond, however, will give little comfort to the mainly French holders of decorative but almost worthless bonds issued during Tsarist rule, which the Bolsheviks refused to honour when they took over the country almost 80 years ago.
"Russia has never declared responsibility for the debt issued during the Tsarist period," Livshits said.
Talks with the French government on the issue are for "mutual claims" only and Moscow was not involved in paying money to individual owners of Tsarist bonds, he added.
